sermon:
A man writes a letter to people who have lost their homes. James addresses it to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion — believers scattered by persecution, refugees with the salt of grief still on their faces. And the first thing he says to them is the last thing they expect. Not a word of comfort. A command to count.

**The trial is not the absence of God**

"Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness" (James 1:2-3). Notice what he does not say. He does not say the trials are an accident. He does not say they are a punishment, the withdrawal of favor, the proof that God has gone quiet. He says they are doing something. The testing produces. The fire is not destroying the faith; it is finishing it. James reaches for the image of metal in the furnace, where the heat is the only thing that drives the dross to the surface so it can be skimmed away.

This cuts against everything we feel when the trial arrives. We read suffering as evidence — evidence that we have done something wrong, or that God has done nothing at all. James says read it the other way. The God who lets your faith be tested has not stepped back. He is at the work of your maturity, and maturity is the thing you cannot reach any other path.

**Wisdom for the one who asks**

But a tested man does not always know what the test is for. So James says: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him" (James 1:5). Without reproach. God does not sigh when you ask. He does not hold your earlier failures over the request. He gives, James says, generously, to all — and the only thing that disqualifies the asking is the double mind, the man who prays for wisdom while keeping one hand on his own plan, tossed like a wave because he has not decided whom he trusts.

Then comes the turn that the whole chapter has been building toward. James will not let faith stay in the head. "Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves" (James 1:22). He gives us the man at the mirror who sees his own face and walks away and forgets what he looks like. That is the hearer. He had the truth in front of him long enough to be changed by it, and he was not changed, and the strangest part is that he does not know it. The deception is self-administered. We are very good at mistaking the experience of hearing for the fact of having.

I feel the indictment land on the preacher first. I have stood under more sermons than I have ever obeyed. I have wept at truth on a Sunday and lived as though I had never heard it by Tuesday. The man at the mirror is not the skeptic in the back row. He is me, comfortable in the second pew, moved and unmoved at once. James says pure religion is not the feeling. It is visiting the widow and the orphan in their affliction, and keeping yourself unstained. Religion you can see, or no religion at all.

**Where this points**

And here is the thing the scattered believers needed and we need. The Christ this letter serves was Himself tested in every respect, and through what He suffered He was made the pioneer of our salvation. He counted the joy set before Him while He endured the cross. The wisdom James tells us to ask for has a name and a face — Christ became to us wisdom from God. So when we ask, we are not reaching into the dark for a quality. We are asking the Father to give us more of His Son. The doing James demands is not how we earn the word. It is the only honest proof that the word has gotten inside us, the way the resurrection got inside the men who hid behind locked doors and then would not stop speaking.

Do not walk away from the mirror. Do the word you heard today, the one specific thing, before the feeling fades.

Hearing is not having.

Picture the door of the assembly. Two men come in on the same morning. One wears gold rings and fine clothing; the other is poor, in shabby clothes, smelling of the road. James says you watch what the church does next. You give the gold rings the good seat. You tell the poor man to stand over there, or sit on the floor by your feet. And James names it before you can dress it up as hospitality. "Have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?" (James 2:4).

**Partiality contradicts the God you claim**

He begins by tying it to the name. "My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory" (James 2:1). You cannot hold faith in the Lord of glory and run a seating chart by income. The two will not sit together. Because the God you confess made His choice in the other direction. "Has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith?" The very people the church shames at the door are the people God selected to inherit the kingdom. To honor the rich man over the poor is not merely bad manners. It is to set yourself against the preference of God Himself, to despise the one He elected.

And notice the realism. James is not romanticizing the poor and demonizing the rich as a class. He is naming what the assembly actually did — it leaned toward power, toward the man who could help the church, toward the ring that signaled he was worth keeping. We do this. I do this. I have felt the small internal calculation when an influential visitor walks in, the warmth that arrives unearned, and the way that same warmth is harder to summon for the person who needs us and can give nothing back. That calculation is the sin James is hunting.

**The law is not a buffet**

Then he closes the escape route. We would like to think partiality is a minor failing, a rough edge on an otherwise good record. James will not allow it. "For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become accountable for all of it" (James 2:10). The law is not a list of separate boxes where a clean score elsewhere covers one omission. It is a single garment; tear it at one seam and you have torn the garment. The same God who said do not commit adultery said do not show partiality. Break the second and you have broken with the Lawgiver, not just the line.

This is meant to wound our self-grading. We keep an internal ledger where the sins of welcome and exclusion rank far below the sins we name from the pulpit. James files them together. The royal law, love your neighbor as yourself, is fulfilled or it is fractured, and the man at your door is your neighbor whether or not he can repay you.

**Mercy with a face**

Where does this drive us. To the only mercy that can be shown to people who have shown so little. James ends: "For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment" (James 2:13). That is not first a threat. It is the gospel in miniature. The Lord of glory James named at the start did not take the good seat. He had no place to lay His head. He came to the poor, ate with the unwanted, and was Himself shown no mercy at the cross so that mercy could triumph over the judgment we earned at our own doors.

A church that has received that mercy cannot run a welcome mat that sorts people by their clothes. We were the shabby ones. We were brought in off the road and given the good seat we could not afford. So we speak and act as people who will be judged under the law of liberty — which means we extend the welcome we were given, especially to the one who can do nothing for us.

Go home and find the person your warmth skips. Greet that one first.

Mercy triumphs over judgment.

A brother is cold. A sister has nothing to eat. They are standing in front of you, and you say to them, "Go in peace, be warmed and filled," and you give them nothing — no coat, no bread, no shelter from the cold you just blessed them out of. James asks the only honest question. "What good is that?" (James 2:16). The words were warm. The man went away cold. And James uses that scene as the picture of a kind of faith we do not like to look at directly.

**Faith that produces nothing produces nothing**

"What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?" (James 2:14). Read the wording carefully, because James is precise. He does not say works save. He says a faith that has no works cannot. He is examining the claim, the man who says he has faith. James is asking whether the saying is true, and he gives us a test no claim can dodge: the evidence. "Faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead."

Then he raises the stakes past the human level. "You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe — and shudder" (James 2:19). This is the verse that should empty the room of every false comfort. Right doctrine is not the dividing line between the saved and the lost. The demons have flawless theology. They have never doubted the existence of God for a single second of their existence, and their orthodoxy buys them nothing but terror. A creed you can recite while your life contradicts it is a creed you share with hell.

**Abraham and Rahab — faith completed**

James does not leave us with abstraction. He calls two witnesses, and they could not be less alike. Abraham, the father of the nation, offered his son Isaac on the altar, and James says his faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works. Then Rahab — a Gentile, a prostitute, a woman with no standing — who received the spies and sent them out another way. One is the patriarch. The other is an outsider with a scandalous past. James puts them side by side to say living faith looks the same in both: it does something. It moves. The faith and the act were not two things; the act was the faith made visible.

Then the verdict that closes the section: "For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead" (James 2:26). A body without breath is a corpse. It may have every feature it had in life — the same face, the same hands. What it does not have is the one thing that made it alive. James says that is exactly what faith without works is. Not weak faith. Dead faith. A corpse of a creed.

**The self-examination we avoid**

This is where I have to stop preaching and stand under it. It is possible to defend the doctrine of justification by faith alone with great skill and to have a faith that has never once cost me anything, never fed anyone, never moved my schedule or my checkbook. James is not letting me grade my faith by what I affirm. He is making me grade it by what it has produced. And when I look honestly, I find seasons where my faith was orthodox and inert — a believing that shuddered at nothing and served no one.

And yet the Christ this faith trusts is precisely the One whose faith was not inert. He did not say to us, go in peace, be warmed and filled. He clothed us in His own righteousness and fed us with His body. The works James demands are the fruit, never the root; the root is a Savior who acted when words would have been cheaper. Faith that has hold of that Christ cannot stay still, because He did not.

Look for the breath. If your faith has never moved, it may never have lived.

Dead faith saves no one.

You have watched a fire start from nothing. A single match dropped in dry grass, and by evening a hillside is gone. James says that is your tongue. Small as the match, and capable of the same ruin. "How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire" (James 3:5). He has just warned that not many should become teachers, because teachers are judged with greater strictness, and then he widens it to every one of us, because the smallest member of the body does the largest damage.

**Small member, whole course**

James stacks the images. A bit in a horse's mouth turns the whole animal. A small rudder steers a great ship against strong winds. Both are tiny; both govern something vast. So the tongue. It is a little member, and it boasts of great things, and it sets on fire the entire course of a person's life. He goes further than damage to others. The tongue sets ablaze the course of the one who speaks. The words that come out of you do not only burn the people they land on. They burn back along the wire into your own life, shaping the man who said them.

Then the verdict that should sober every one of us who has ever tried to manage our speech by willpower. "No human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison" (James 3:8). Men have tamed lions, James says, and birds, and creatures of the sea. The one thing no man has tamed is the muscle behind his own teeth. If you have ever resolved to do better with your words and found yourself, by the end of the week, saying the thing you swore you would not say, James is not surprised. He told you it could not be tamed by you.

**The divided spring**

Now he reaches the thing he has been driving at. "With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so" (James 3:9-10). Here is the horror of it laid bare. The same mouth. The voice that sang the hymn this morning is the voice that shredded a person at lunch, and the person at lunch was made in the image of the God the hymn praised. You cannot curse the image without aiming at the One it images.

Then the question from nature that exposes us. Does a spring pour both fresh water and salt from the same opening? Can a fig tree bear olives, or a grapevine figs? No. The fountain is judged by what comes out of it. And James means for us to feel the diagnosis: a mouth that blesses and curses is not revealing two moods. It is revealing one divided heart. The tongue is not the disease. It is the thermometer. What comes out was already inside.

**What the mouth tells**

This is where I cannot hide behind the office of preacher. I am most fluent in the words I most regret. The sermon and the sharp remark come out of the same throat, and James says that is not hypocrisy I can fix by trying harder at the level of the lips. The spring needs changing. And there is only One who changes springs. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, Jesus said, and He is the only one who gives a new heart from which the abundance can be different. The tongue no man can tame is tamed, slowly and from the inside, by the Spirit of Christ remaking the fountain.

So do not start with your words this week. Start with the heart they are reporting on, and take it to the only One who can make a spring run fresh. But do not pretend the words do not matter, or that they are not telling the truth about you. They are. They always were.

Your mouth tells the truth.

Everyone in the room thinks they are wise. James does not argue with the claim directly. He does something harder. He says: show me. "Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom" (James 3:13). Not by his arguments. Not by how much he knows. By his conduct, and specifically by its meekness. Wisdom, James says, is not a thing you assert. It is a thing that shows, the way a tree shows by its fruit which kind of tree it is.

**The wisdom from below**

Then he tells us there are two kinds, and they look more alike from the outside than we would expect. The first he describes without flattery. "But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic" (James 3:14-15). Three words, and they climb downward. Earthly — it belongs to this world and no further. Unspiritual — it comes from the natural self, not the Spirit. Demonic — it shares the source of the enemy. James is willing to say that a cleverness driven by jealousy and ambition is not merely lesser wisdom. It is hell's wisdom wearing a respectable face.

And you know it by what it breeds. "Where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice." That is the tell. This wisdom is real, it is effective, it wins arguments and builds platforms — and it leaves disorder in its wake. Look at the field behind a man. If it is full of broken relationships and faction and chaos he calls righteous zeal, you have found the demonic wisdom, however smart it sounded. I have to ask whether the disorder I have sometimes left in my own ministry was the residue of a wisdom I was proud of and should have feared.

**The wisdom from above**

Against this James sets the other. "But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere" (James 3:17). Read the order. First pure, then peaceable. The heavenly wisdom does not buy peace by selling out purity, and it does not enforce purity by trampling peace. It holds both, in that sequence. And then the run of qualities, every one of them relational — gentle, open to reason, full of mercy, impartial, sincere. This is not the wisdom of the man who is always right. It is the wisdom of the man you can disagree with and still be safe near.

The contrast is the whole sermon. Both kinds of wisdom can sound intelligent. The difference is not IQ. It is the harvest. "And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace." Earthly wisdom sows division and reaps disorder. Heavenly wisdom sows in peace and reaps righteousness. You are not known by what you claim to be wise about. You are known by what grows in the ground around your life.

**The wisdom with a name**

And here is where it stops being a contrast of qualities and becomes a person. The wisdom from above came down from above. It has a face. Christ is the wisdom of God, and look at the list again — pure, peaceable, gentle, merciful, impartial, sincere. That is not a description of an abstraction. That is His portrait. To ask for wisdom from above, as chapter one told us to, is to ask to be made like Him. The meekness of wisdom is the meekness of the One who was meek and lowly in heart, who made peace by His own blood.

So do not measure your wisdom by your certainty. Measure it by the harvest. Walk back through the rooms you have left this week and ask what grew there — peace, or disorder. The fruit is not lying about the root.

Wisdom is known by fruit.

James asks a question that is too blunt for polite religion. "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?" (James 4:1). Not among you, first. Within you. The conflict you are having with that person — the standoff in the family, the faction in the church — James traces it past the other person, past the circumstance, all the way down to a war being fought inside your own chest. The fight out there is the overflow of a fight in here.

**The war inside the prayerlessness**

Then he says the thing that should stop us cold. "You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask" (James 4:2). Look at the diagnosis. The reason you do not have the thing you are fighting to seize is not that God withheld it. It is that you never asked Him for it. You went to war for what you would not pray for. And when prayer does happen, James says, it is often corrupted at the source: "You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions." The prayer becomes another tool of the appetite, the divine vending machine for the same cravings that started the war.

This is the kind of self-examination I avoid. I would rather analyze the conflict, assign the blame, build the case against the other party. James turns me around to face the desire that is driving me, the want that has set itself up as a small god, and the prayer life that went silent precisely where I was most determined to get my way.

**Friendship that is enmity**

Now comes the verse that names the real allegiance underneath. "You adulterous people, do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God" (James 4:4). Adulterous — because James is using the old prophetic language of a covenant people sleeping with someone other than their husband. This is not the world as planet or people. It is the world as a system of values that leaves God out, the order of things that prizes what the passions prize. And James will not let it be neutral. You cannot be its friend and His. Friendship with one is enmity with the other. There is no treaty.

We want a middle territory, a way to love what the world loves and keep God too. James says it does not exist, and the reason is jealousy — "He yields the Spirit he has made to dwell in us" with a holy jealousy. He will not share you. And that should not feel like a threat once you understand it; it is the jealousy of a husband, not a tyrant.

**The only way back is down**

So what is the way home for an adulterous, quarreling, prayerless people. Not up. Down. "But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble" (James 4:6). There is the hinge of the whole chapter. More grace, always more grace, but it runs downhill — it pools where a man has lowered himself, and it slides off the proud who stand too tall to catch it. Then the commands come in a rush: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near, cleanse, mourn, weep. "Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you" (James 4:10).

And this is the gospel pattern with a name on it. Christ did not grasp at equality with God but humbled Himself, even to death on a cross, and therefore God exalted Him. The way down that James commands is the way his own Lord walked. We do not climb to God over the bodies of the people we are fighting. We go low, where the grace already is, where the Savior already went. The proud get opposed. The lowly get lifted, by the nail-marked hands.

Stop fighting for it. Get on your knees and ask for it.

Humble yourself. He lifts.

James turns and speaks past the church to the rich who have been grinding it down. "Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you" (James 5:1). The charge is specific. They have hoarded wealth in the last days. They have held back the wages of the laborers who mowed their fields, and James says the wages are crying out, and the cries have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. This is not a sermon against money. It is a sermon against fraud — against luxury built on a withheld paycheck, fattening hearts in a day of slaughter while the worker who earned it goes hungry.

**Judgment stored, patience required**

The point for the suffering church is the next word: therefore. "Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord" (James 5:7). Because judgment is stored up — because the cries have been heard and the Judge is standing at the door — the defrauded believer does not have to seize justice with his own hands. He can wait. James gives the farmer as the picture: he waits for the precious fruit of the earth, patient over it until it gets the early and the late rains. The farmer cannot make it rain. He cannot pull the harvest up faster by force. He works, and he waits, and he trusts the timing of heaven over the ground.

That is the posture for the wronged. Not passivity, but patience with a reason — "the coming of the Lord is at hand." The waiting is not empty. It is leaning toward a date that God has fixed and we have not been told, and James says establish your hearts, because the One you are waiting for is near.

**The church that prays through the waiting**

But James does not leave the waiting church idle. He fills the wait with prayer, and the range of it is striking. "Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise. Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord" (James 5:13-14). Every condition routes back to God. The suffering pray, the glad sing, the sick send for the elders. The church waits on its knees, not its heels.

And then the promise that has carried the praying church for two thousand years. "The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working" (James 5:16). James reaches for Elijah, and is careful to say he was a man with a nature like ours — not a superhuman, a man like us — who prayed, and the sky shut for three years, and prayed again, and it opened. James means us to believe that the prayer of an ordinary believer moves the hand of God. Over the sick. Over sin, confessed to one another. Over the brother who wanders from the truth and is brought back, his soul saved from death.

**The one we are waiting for**

I need to be honest about where this finds me. I am better at seizing than at waiting, better at managing the injustice than at entrusting it. And I pray less than I preach about prayer. James puts the suffering church and the praying church in the same chapter to say they are the same church — the people who wait well are the people who pray, because waiting without prayer curdles into bitterness, and prayer without waiting curdles into demand.

The coming of the Lord James points to is the return of the One who was Himself defrauded, whose own wages were thirty pieces of silver, who was patient under suffering all the way to a cross and did not call down the legions He could have called. He waited, trusting the Father's vindication, and on the third day He was vindicated. So the church waits in His pattern, prays in His name, and leans toward His appearing. The Judge at the door is the Savior who bled. That is why we can be patient, and why we can pray.

The rain is coming. Keep praying.

Be patient. He is near.
